parole.significato: ending of colloquial hypocoristic feminine names
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek -ω (-ō) of feminine proper names, from the vocative of Slavic names taken as nominative, also applied to common feminine nouns.
From a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *vydra, from Proto-Indo-European *údreh₂. Doublet of Ύδρα (Ýdra) and ύδρα (ýdra).
Inherited from Byzantine Greek καρβέλιν (karbélin), or γαρβέλιν (garbélin), from Slavic or Aromanian cârveli, plural of cârveale. Cognate to Albanian karabele (“bread for soldiers”).
Borrowed from Slavic котац (kɔ̌tat͡s: pigsty) + -ι (-i), from Proto-Slavic *kotьcь (“nest, warehouse”).

From Byzantine Greek κουτάβιον (koutábion), of uncertain further origin. Perhaps from an element (*kut-) of Slavic origin (compare Bulgarian ку́че (kúče, “dog”)) + a suffix -άβιον (-ávion). Likely not related to κόττᾰβος (kóttăbos, “cottabus (game)”).

Inherited from Byzantine Greek ροῦχον (roûkhon), borrowed from a Slavic language; see Proto-Slavic *ruxo (“garments, clothing”) (whence Serbo-Croatian ruho, Polish rucho) for more.
